title: Equity-promoting integer programming approaches for medical resident rotation scheduling
contribution: Feasibility, equity-neutral and bi-objective equity-promoting IP models for resident rotation and vacation scheduling, an exact Pareto Search Algorithm (keep previous grants, add one to the worst-off resident) that finds whole Pareto fronts where the epsilon-constraint method fails within a day, and a web tool built with the collaborating residency program.
problem_entry: A collaborator's manual, weeks-long scheduling task; a blind feasible assignment leaves residents unequally served in vacation requests; few prior models make equity a formal objective or allow class-specific block lengths (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: Bracket the bi-objective integer front with two lexicographic solves (Props 1-2), then step one granted request at a time with an IP that fixes previous grants and grants one to a least-served resident (Props 3-4), falling back to the full epsilon-problem when infeasible (pp. 12-14).
assumptions: All program/ACGME/vacation rules are hard constraints; equity only on number of granted vacation requests; seven linearizable inequity measures; 18 instances from 2018-2023 structures with synthetic requests (rules A, B) plus a 2023-2024 case with 54 residents; data not public (pp. 9-10, 15-16, 39).
proof_devices: Props 1-2: lexicographic solves give the two ends of the Pareto front (p. 12; proofs pp. 23-24)
integrality of f1: consecutive non-dominated points differ by >= 1 request, so epsilon = 1 is exact (Remark 1, pp. 11-12)
Prop 3 per inequity measure via the request-distribution vector k and differences psi(k') - psi(k) (pp. 13-14; proof pp. 23-29, skimmed)
Prop 4 by induction over Step 3: restricted and full problems have equal optimal f2 (p. 14; proof p. 30, skimmed)
count of extra variables/constraints per measure linearization explains run-time ranking (Table 7, p. 24; p. 21)
experiments: Gurobi 9.5 on a MacBook Pro M1 (the chief resident's hardware). Pareto fronts for five measures on the case instance (3 to 63 non-dominated points), price of equity 0-0.44, integrated vs sequential practice approach with three distinct rotation solutions (sequential dominated), resident- vs class-based equity, 90 timing runs: all fronts in about 2 h or less ('less than two hours' in the text, max 7972 s in Table 6), while epsilon-constraint solves none under Gini/MeanDev/SumMaxPair within a day (pp. 15-21, 36).
positioning: Builds on resident-scheduling literature (Erhard, Guo, Bard, Smalley-Keskinocak, Proano-Agarwal); claims varied block structures, a choice of inequity measures, a full-front exact algorithm and a decision-support tool; criticism is mild (pp. 3-5, 11).
writing: OR-application style: methodological and practical contributions, 'insights' lists, propositions in the main text with proofs in the E-Companion; one slip (Section 7.3 promised as 'manual approach', delivered as sequential approach) (pp. 2-3, 11, 15, 17-19).
limits_future: No clear winner among inequity measures, no universal answer on individual vs group equity, data not public; future: uncertainty such as absenteeism and equity in shift scheduling; not stated: synthetic requests in the timing instances, no deployment results (pp. 15-22, 39).

title: A Proximal-Gradient Method for Solving Regularized Optimization Problems with General Constraints
contribution: A penalty-free proximal-gradient method with normal/tangential step decomposition and an l2 merit function for min f + r s.t. c(x) = 0, x >= 0, with O(eps^-2) complexity without a CQ (to infeasibility stationarity) and under a sequential CQ (to KKT), global convergence under LICQ at limit points, and active-set and manifold identification; it beats Bazinga on 81 CUTEst-derived and sparse CCA problems (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: Proximal-gradient methods identify structure, but projections onto nonlinear constraints are intractable and penalty methods may destroy structure; existing composite-constrained methods are penalty/AL-based or assume feasible subproblems (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Normal step: Cauchy-decrease solution of a bound-constrained trust-region subproblem on linearized infeasibility with radius kappa_v alpha_k delta_k; tangential step: strongly convex proximal subproblem with Ju = 0, bounds and explicit r (u = 0 always feasible); l2 merit function with a decreasing merit parameter; proximal parameter shrinks on rejection; exit at infeasible stationary points (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Bounded f, c with Lipschitz bounded gradients on an open convex set containing the iterates, convex r with bounded subdifferential (Assumption 3.1, p. 6); layered: no CQ; sequential CQ on [J_k; I_A] uniformly (Assumption 5.1, p. 15); bounded X and LICQ at limit points (pp. 18); strict complementarity (p. 24); partial smoothness, nondegeneracy and alpha bounded below (p. 25).
proof_devices: Cauchy-decrease lemma for projected backtracking adapted from More [41], three cases (Lemma 4.3, pp. 7-8)
stationarity measure using ||v_k(1)|| instead of ||c_k|| when no CQ is assumed (5.1, p. 11)
merit-parameter lower bound when decreased, eps_tau ||v_k(1)||^2 (Lemma 5.5, p. 12), giving the dichotomy Theorem 5.8 (p. 14)
monotone shifted merit function from [16] and telescoping for O(eps^-2) (Lemma 5.7, Theorem 5.8, pp. 13-15)
sequential CQ converts infeasibility stationarity to ||c_k|| (Lemma 5.9, p. 15) for Theorem 5.12 (p. 17)
compact limit set plus finite ball cover for uniform singular-value bounds (Lemmas 5.17-5.19, pp. 20-21); eventual merit-parameter and multiplier bounds (Lemmas 5.22, 5.24, pp. 22-24)
active-set identification from subproblem complementarity under strict complementarity (Theorem 5.26, pp. 24-25)
manifold identification by verifying the hypotheses of a partial-smoothness theorem [37, Thm 4.10] (Theorem 5.27, pp. 25-26)
experiments: Python with Gurobi subproblem solvers; implemented alpha update differs from the analysed one (stated); 81 CUTEst problems reformulated with an artificial l1-weighted variable a whose zero is a KKT point by construction (lambda = ||y_eq||_inf + 10 from IPOPT), filtered on IPOPT success; six-column table vs Bazinga (71 vs 67 feasible, 70 vs 58 KKT, 76 vs 55 a = 0) and a wall-clock profile; sparse CCA with planted support (sl = 0 everywhere, sparser and faster than Bazinga); single runs; tolerances 1e-4 for Algorithm 3.1 vs 1e-6 for Bazinga; Python vs Julia timing (pp. 26-31).
positioning: Extends [16] (equality constraints only) to bounds; positioned against AL and penalty-barrier methods [8, 17, 18, 26, 38, 46] and non-penalty methods [7, 51] with a specific weakness named for each; Bazinga is called the only open-source code for the problem; claims to be the first PG-type method for this class (pp. 2-3, 27, 31).
writing: Contributions listed as three algorithmic properties and five theorem-numbered results; inequality chains justified step by step; candid about a missing reference and about the implementation departing from the theory; one-paragraph conclusion without future work; small slips ('More-Dolen', Bazinga's time limit attributed to Algorithm 3.1) (pp. 3, 9, 12, 27, 29, 31).
limits_future: No stated limitations or future work; visible: complexity CQ is an assumption on the iterates, manifold identification assumes alpha bounded below, first-order only, n <= 100; unstated: asymmetric tolerances, cross-language timing, filtering on IPOPT success without pre-filter count (pp. 15, 25, 27-29, 31).

title: Fair supervised learning through constraints on smooth nonconvex unfairness-measure surrogates
contribution: Bounded smooth nonconvex surrogates (scaled sigmoid and a Chen-smoothed step) imposed as hard constraints and trained with the authors' stochastic SQP make imposed disparate-impact targets match the achieved ones on Dutch, Law and ACSIncome, with mild accuracy loss and multiple simultaneous measures, unlike regularization or covariance surrogates (arXiv v3 read).
problem_entry: Convex (covariance) surrogates do not bound the true unfairness measure and regularization weights are costly to tune and nonmonotone; Theorem 2.1 (from Yao et al. [43]) bounds the true DP violation for bounded saturating surrogates, but [43] never enforced it as a constraint (pp. 2, 6).
key_idea: Bounded, smooth, nonconvex surrogates scaled so values saturate near 0/1, imposed as hard constraints in the training problem, solved by stochastic SQP with active-set enumeration and stratified mini-batches (pp. 7-9, 23-25).
assumptions: Binary sensitive feature and label (extension asserted), independence criterion, thresholded network output; Theorem 2.1 needs every point's surrogate within gamma of 0 or 1 (approximated by scaling, not enforced); fixed group counts per batch for unbiasedness; SQP theory deferred to [13] (pp. 4-9, 19-20).
proof_devices: Theorem 2.1 proof: odd shift phi -> 2phi - 1, split groups by predicted label, reverse triangle inequality; appendix corrects the bound to 2gamma + eps vs eps + gamma in the main text (pp. 6, 17-19)
Theorem 2.2: covariance surrogate = N0 N1 / N^2 times the linear-phi DP surrogate, hence unbounded and outside Theorem 2.1 (pp. 6-7)
unbiasedness of the group-difference estimate under stratified sampling by linearity of expectation (Theorem 3.1, pp. 9, 19-20)
experiments: Dutch, Law, ACSIncome (50k subset), small networks, 500 epochs full batch, training-data results (test said similar); imposed delta vs achieved delta-hat for surrogate and true measure, unscaled vs scaled (alpha = 50 chosen from six values by minimizing that gap); constraint-only (8 delta) vs regularization-only (8 lambda, nonmonotone); DI + EI together (ACSIncome 78.9% -> 78.5%); 5 seeds mean +/- sd; compute table shows constraint runs up to ~2.5x slower on ACSIncome; label-implied fairness baselines (pp. 9-13, 21-31).
positioning: Against regularization (Kamishima, Bechavod-Ligett) and convex/covariance surrogates (Zafar [44]); alongside constrained fair ML (Donini, Cotter); builds on Yao et al. [43] for the bound and on the authors' [13] for the solver; claims to be the first to combine hard constraints with smooth nonconvex surrogates so the bounds are realized (pp. 2-3, 6-7).
writing: Lettered advantages in the abstract, bold 'first paper' claim, informal theorem in the main text with formal version in the appendix; several v3 inconsistencies (bound eps + gamma vs 2gamma + eps, main text citing appendix Figures 6-9, 'Adult' for ACSIncome, Law N 20,798 vs 16,638, d_lu listed twice) (pp. 1, 3, 6, 9-11, 19, 21-24).
limits_future: Only stated limit: slightly higher training cost outweighed by tuning savings; no future work section; unstated: both approaches ran 8 hyperparameter values so tuning savings are argued not measured, alpha tuned on the evaluation gap, training-data reporting, ~2.5x cost on ACSIncome (pp. 10-11, 13, 27).
